purpose: Methoxsalen is used to treat certain skin conditions like psoriasis, vitiligo (patches of lost skin color), and a type of skin lymphoma called mycosis fungoides. It is also used to help skin become more tolerant to sunlight in people with certain light-sensitive conditions. It works best when combined with ultraviolet A (UVA) light therapy, a treatment called PUVA.
how_it_works: Methoxsalen makes your skin extra sensitive to ultraviolet A light. When UVA light hits skin that has this medicine in it, it slows down the rapid growth of abnormal skin cells and helps reduce inflammation. Think of it like a key that only activates when the right light shines on it, targeting problem areas in your skin.
common_side_effects: Nausea and upset stomach are the most common side effects, especially when taken by mouth. You may also notice redness, itching, or burning of the skin after light treatment. Dizziness and headache can sometimes occur as well.
warnings: This medicine makes your skin and eyes very sensitive to sunlight for at least 8 to 24 hours after taking it — you must wear UV-protective sunglasses and protect your skin from the sun during this time. Long-term use increases the risk of skin cancer and eye damage, so regular check-ups are very important. Do not use it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and avoid it if you have lupus or certain other light-sensitive conditions. Never take extra doses or use a sun lamp unless your doctor tells you to.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on your body weight and the condition being treated. For oral use, it is usually taken 1.5 to 2 hours before your scheduled UVA light therapy session. Treatments are typically given 2 to 3 times per week, never on back-to-back days. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose that is right for you.
